title: Perception
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of cultivating compassion and understanding in our interactions with others by being aware of our own perceptions and reactions. Nomon Tim Burnett invites the audience to explore perception as a process that involves noticing suffering, feeling empathy, and staying with it, rather than just offering abstract support. By recognizing how our individual perspectives can lead to misunderstandings and frustration, we can work towards greater compassion and understanding for ourselves and others.

sentences.text: Well, first, a few notes and appreciations.
I hope, like me, you're really appreciating our sangha.
What a nice group of people, huh?
Devoted to whatever the heck this is, even though they don't exactly know whatever the heck this is.
Because it helps us, and we help each other, and we help the people in our lives, by spending some time just being.
It's the strangest thing in the world that sitting around doing nothing results in your heart opening and healing.
Who would have thought that?
I also want to appreciate everyone who came last Saturday.
I was off working, but I know there was a very productive and fun morning of practice and work party.
We have the Weed-O-Meter to tell us whether there was a work party or not.
The Weed-O-Meter dialed back.
So, anyway, thanks for coming if you came.
If you weren't able to come to that one, we're intending to have another work day on July 2nd, I think, this first Saturday of July.
Also, a little note about the Wednesday night schedule coming up.
There's just a fabulous lineup of brilliant speakers.
Next week, Edie's going to give a talk on a koan that we studied.
The week after that, during the Samish sesshin, some of us will be gone in Samish, some of us will be here, so things continue here.
The regular schedule continues.
Andrea Thatch will give a talk.
The week after that, we'll have our quarterly sangha conversation, so we'll have a chance to have a discussion and reflection on how we're doing and what's going on in the sangha.
And the board has some things it wants to share.
Coupled with that, on June 29th, we'll have a nice little ceremony we do with those quarterly.
It's the fifth Wednesday of the month, so sort of automatically it's quarterly, more or less.
Anyway, we'll also have a ceremony to thank and appreciate new members, newly joined or recently joined members.
People who haven't gotten around to doing the ceremony could even have been a member for 20 years.
I don't know, but if you haven't done this ceremony yet, you're welcome.
We like to get to thank you.
And then it just continues from there.
In July, the four Wednesdays of July, and I'll be gone for a chunk of that.
I usually take a sabbatical in July.
Andrea is organizing a four-week seminar on early woman Buddhist ancestors.
So the schedule will be a little lighter on meditation and have more time for talk and discussion and interaction.
She will get it on the website soon, but she's picked out four really interesting woman ancestors to bring up.
And maybe there'll be readings.
I don't know what else she's going to do, but it'll be cool.
So just carry on.
Then sometime in August, we will get to hear a report, we hope, from our three pilgrims who just returned from Japan: Hannah and John and Bob.
That'll be delightful.
I hear they took a couple of pictures.
And then woven into that, the hiking retreat events are starting to happen.
Please check the website or look on the bulletin board for those dates.
Day hike in the middle of July and an expedition to the old growth the first Saturday in August.
And a four, five-day retreat and backpack in the second week of August, third week of August.
So check that out.
It seems like we're doing a lot of stuff, and it's all really lovely stuff.
In September, a five-day sesshin with Seattle so-and-so.
We could go on and on.
And Jonathan Riopel is training up to help us stay informed and clear on all the events.
He's putting them on the website and he's sending announcements.
So you may have gotten an announcement in the email about the Dharma talks that are open to go for a visit during our annual eight-day retreat coming up.
Week after, week after next?
Two weeks from now.
So that was Jonathan's work.
Anyway, little by little, we get organized.
Well, I've been continuing to try to think and study and practice compassion as I can.
It's a little daunting sometimes, because I just notice how self-absorbed I'm actually conditioned to be.
You notice that?
I don't know if you feel that way, but most of the dialogue is me, me, me, what do I need today?
It's good to take care of myself, but I notice sometimes I pull away from engagement, real engagement with others.
It's just this habit thing.
So I've been thinking about compassion as a process.
It's not exactly a virtuousness or being a good person.
I've been thinking about compassion as a process, which is nice, because if it's a process, we can identify different steps in it and work on them and practice with them.
The first step in the process of compassion seems to be to actually notice that somebody's suffering.
So it's an active perception, whether that's somebody else that we're in relationship with or ourselves; we're worthy of compassion too.
And there's a funny gloss there.
Like I was just saying, it troubles me sometimes that it's just me, me, me, me.
But then there's also this other way of being with me, this putative me that's a little different, that's in touch with my suffering, that's softer, that's wiser: that's self-compassion.
So self-concern seems to be a little problematic, but self-compassion is so beautiful.
It's funny.
So the first step would be perception, actually noticing that somebody's suffering.
And the second step would be actually feeling something about that.
So not just an abstract idea, like, "Oh, she's suffering, sorry, too bad for you, stay over there," but actually feeling something.
This is empathy, the felt sense of connection.
Apparently our brains are wired up to mirror the feeling in the other if we pay attention in our own body.
There's a subtle way that we can feel the same pain in our own body that that person is feeling, strangely enough.
So then we feel some pain.
Compassion means to suffer with somebody.
There's lots of other kinds of helping, but compassion involves this quality of noticing the suffering, being willing to feel the suffering, and then being willing to stay with it.
Then we don't leave, because there are so many exit points in this process, right?
Like, "OK, ouch, thank you, goodbye."
Be willing to stay.
And then we seem to do some kind of internal assessment: can I handle this?
Is this within my capabilities?
Some sort of resource thing happens in our hearts and our minds.
Is this too much for me?
I may be willing to help, but what if it's just too much?

And then eventually we can just be compassionate, just be with the suffering of another or the suffering of ourselves, with a willingness to help, a willingness to stay put, a willingness to be open, a willingness to be kind.
That may manifest in some kind of action.
We don't always know what kind of action.
Sometimes that action is maybe just being present, right?
It doesn't necessarily mean we run around and muck with things.
Maybe other times that action is changing something or doing something.
So anyway, I thought tonight we would look at perception a little bit, because perception all by itself is kind of tricky.
I have three stories of perception.
Then I think we'll have time to have a little conversation about what you've noticed about perception.
The first story, I don't know if it has a real basis or if it's just made up.
I'm just going to tell the story; I don't have it written down.
One time, after a very long day, a tough day at work, this woman goes to a cafe to relax, to recover.
She really loves cookies; cookies are an important comfort food.
That morning, figuring she might need it after a day like this, she had put a bag of cookies in her bag.
At the cafe, there's a bar kind of counter, and she decides to sit there and sip her espresso and eat her cookies.
She sits down next to this other guy, and she starts into her routine of recovering and relaxing and taking care of herself with her espresso and her cookies.
To her shock, this other guy sitting next to her reaches into her cookie bag and takes one of her cookies.
He doesn't say anything, doesn't look at her, just takes one of the cookies.
The cookie bag is in between the two of them.
That's funny.
She's polite and confused and tired, so she takes a cookie.
Maybe he's not going to do it again, this weirdo.
But then he does it again; he takes another cookie.
And she takes another cookie, and little by little they're silently, with increasing tension and worry on her side, going through the bag.
The whole thing is not relaxing at all, because there's this creep eating the cookies and he's not saying anything.
She's not comfortable saying anything back.
And then, finally, he reaches into the bag, takes up the last cookie, breaks it in half, puts half of it on her plate, eats the other, and turns around and leaves.
It's the weirdest thing.
Exhausted by this whole thing, and strangely touched by that last little action, but confused, she goes back to her car, reaches into her bag for her keys, and finds in her bag her bag of cookies.
Full, an open bag of cookies in her bag.
That was his bag.
Isn't that a funny story?
So, perception, right?
And we've been talking about the precepts a bunch lately, so who was stealing?
And intention, and so on.
So, there's story number one.
Story number two is a story that happened to me.
That's a little shorter.
So, Samish is coming up, which involves a flurry of communications.
Sixty or seventy people are coming, and another ten or twenty wanted to come but didn't, and this, that, and the other thing.
There are various questions and concerns and challenges with money, because it's several hundred dollars, right?
We do it as low as we can, but it's a chunk.
I'm not responding to all these anymore, praise Buddha, but I'm trying to help, and the retreat manager and the registrar are trying to cover these things.
Somehow this one woman just kept falling through the cracks.
She turns out to be connected to our dear friend John Bales, and she lives in Oregon, and she needed some support from us to come to [unclear: "this machine"], so she's been asking.
She sends this long letter, all about Roshi John Bales.
I've never heard of Roshi John Bales, but now we know he's a Roshi.
Anyway, out of desperation she looked me up on the web or something, and now she's writing directly to me, and finally she sends a fairly exasperated message.
I'm trying to be good, so my intention in all this is to be better at not jumping in and doing everything, because that's bad for me, it's bad for the sangha.
So I've been deliberately just forwarding these to the appropriate person, and not answering, and actually removing it from my inbox, and just trusting.
They'll handle it, and most of them do get handled, 99% of them.
But this one lady, for some reason, just went into the cracks.

So finally she sends me directly an exasperated message: "Tim, I don't know what's happening, and I really passionately want to come to the retreat, and I'm not getting answered, and can you please tell me what's going on?"
And then the last line of this email that she sent to me says, "I hope this teaches you."
I hope this teaches you.
I can feel my face get hot, my gut clench a little bit, the jaw get tight, the fingers itching to do some damage on the keyboard.
But luckily, somehow, luck or practice or good mood before that moment, I just pause a little bit, and I say, "Well, I don't know what she means by that.
She is right that we've not responded, so I should just respond to the actual question about Samish.
And this 'teaches you' thing, God knows, but maybe I'll find out, who knows.
I'm just going to set this aside."
I'm not saying it's not pissing me off that this woman said this to me, but I'm not going to respond to that part.
So I respond to her, and sometimes email could be days or two seconds.
This is one of those two-second ones.
She writes right back.
"Oh, thank you so much for responding to me.
I feel so much better.
And by the way, Tim, funny little typo in that email I sent you.
You figured it out?
I meant to write, 'I hope this reaches you.'" So one letter different.
It goes from just an expression of hope to perceived aggression.
So it's interesting.
We're always communicating and trying to, and doing actions, and the actions of all other people, and bags of cookies and assumptions.
How can we be compassionate if we're actually completely different universes about whose bag of cookies it was or what we're saying to each other?
And here's the third one, and then we'll have a discussion about perception.
This is a little story from the wonderful Palestinian-American poet Naomi Shihab Nye.
And by the way, another little sign, I forgot to tell Bob that I went to the Skagit Valley Poetry Festival.
I wasn't able to go to the whole thing, so I didn't actually meet Naomi, but Norman Fischer was there.
So I got to see Norman and hang around with him a little bit.
I was grateful to you and the other organizers.
This is only every other year.
It's the [unclear: "Sleeper Jam"] event of the Northwest every other year in the Skagit Valley in [unclear: "Likana"].
So two years from now, look out for the Skagit Poetry Festival.
Try to go.
It was a beautiful sunny day and it was lovely.
Anyway, Naomi Shihab Nye was there as well as Norman.
I don't doubt she read this story, but I'm going to read it to you now.
It's a little short story called "Museum."
*I was 17.
My family had just moved to San Antonio.
A local magazine featured an alluring article about a museum called the McNay, an old mansion once the home of an eccentric, many-times-married watercolorist named Marion Kugler McNay.
She had deeded it to the community to become a museum after her death, and she had a good art collection.
So I asked my friend Sally, who drove a cute little convertible and who had moved to Texas a year before we did, if she wanted to go there.*
*Sally said, "Sure."
She was a good friend that way.
Sally and I had made up a few words in our own language, and we could dissolve into laughter just by saying them.
Our mothers thought that we were a little bit odd.
But anyway, on a sunny Saturday afternoon, we drove over to Broadway.
Sally asked me, "Do you have the address of this place?"
"No," I said, "just drive slowly and I'll recognize it from the picture in the magazine."*
*I peered in both directions and pointed, saying, "Oh, there it is, pull in."
The parking lot was under some palm trees.
The parking lot was pretty empty.
We entered excited.
The museum was free.
And right away, the spirit of the arched doorways, carved window frames, and the elegant artwork overtook us.
Sally went left.
I went right.
There were a couple of people seated in some chairs in the lobby.
They stopped talking and stared at us when we entered.
"May I help you?" a man said.
"No," I said, "we're fine."
I don't like to talk to people in museums, really.
Tourists and docents really get on my nerves.*
*What if they talked a long time about a painting that you weren't that interested in?
So I took a deep breath and moved on to another painting, fireworks over a patio in Mexico, maybe.
There weren't very good tags in this museum.
In fact, there weren't any tags.
I stood back and gazed.
Sally had gone upstairs.
The people in the lobby had stopped chatting at this point.
They seemed very nosy, keeping their eyes on me with irritating curiosity.
What was their problem?
I turned down a hallway.
Bougainvilles and azaleas pressed up right against the windows.
Maybe we should have brought a picnic.
Was that a Moorish courtyard over there?
I saw some nice sculptures in another room and a small couch.
This would be a great place for reading.*
*Above the couch hung a radiant print by Paul Klee, my favorite artist.
Blues and pinks merging softly in his own wonderful way.
I stepped closer, looking.
Suddenly I was aware of a man from the lobby standing behind me in the doorway.
"Where do you think you are?" he asked.
I turned sharply.
"The McNay Art Museum, of course."
He smiled then and shook his head.
"Sorry to tell you, the McNay is three blocks over on New Braunfield Street.
Take a right when you go out of our driveway and then another right."
"What is this place?"
I asked.
Still confused, he said, "Well, we consider it our home."
My heart jolted.
I raced past him to the bottom of the staircase, calling out, "Sally, come down."
Immediately, urgent.*
*I remember being tempted to shout something in our private language, but we didn't yet have a word for this situation.
Sally came to the top of the stairs smiling happily and said, "You have to come up here.
There's some really good stuff.
There are these antique beds."
"No, Sally, no," I said, as if she were a dog or a baby.
"Get down here, speed it up.
Emergency."
She stepped elegantly down the stairs as if in a museum trance, looking puzzled.
I just couldn't tell her out loud in front of those people what we had done.
I actually pushed her towards the front door, waving my hand at the family in the chairs, saying, "Sorry.
Oh, my God.
Please forgive us.
You have a really nice place."
Sally stared at me.
Out in the parking lot, when I told her, she covered her mouth and doubled over with laughter, shaking.*
*We're still in their yard and I imagine them looking out the windows at us.
Sally couldn't believe how long they let us look around without saying anything.
"It was really friendly of them," she said.
"Get in the car," I said sternly.
The real McNay was fabulous, too.
Splendid.
But we felt a little nervous the whole time we were there.
Van Gogh, Picasso, Tamayo.
This time there were tags.
This time we stayed together in case anything weird happened.
And we never told anyone.
We never told anyone what had happened.*
*Thirty years later, the story is not done.
Thirty years later, a nice-looking woman approached me at a public gathering.
"Excuse me," she said, "I need to ask you a strange question.
Did you ever, by any chance, enter a residence long ago thinking it was the McNay Museum?"
Thirty years later, my cheeks still burned.
"Yes, but how do you know?
I never told anyone."
"That was my home," she said.
"I was a teenager sitting with my family, talking in the living room.
Before you came over, I never realized what a beautiful place I lived in.
I never felt how lucky I was before and what good taste my parents had.
You thought it was a museum.
My feelings changed about my family after that.
They had good taste.
They took care of me.
And I've always wanted to thank you."
Sometimes our errors of perception can actually result in a lot of good.*
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** So I thought I'd bring up these three stories.
I don't have a particular way of opening the conversation, just to think about how is it for you, perceiving things?
We do this so automatically, right?

And when we're believing that something is the way that it is, we're basically convinced that we're right, until we receive evidence to the contrary, at which point we may just ignore that evidence, keep going, or deny it, or argue, or suddenly have a shift.
And it's so interesting to me, too, the way when perception shifts, what a powerful moment that is.
And often there's a great deal of energy, really.
I didn't say this part of it when I got the "I hope this reaches you" part of my email exchange.
I laughed out loud.
It's just a great release of energy. [unclear: "Maybe she had nice, in case the energy was a little more intense"].
Who knows?
Our imagined lady with her cookies in her purse, how she felt.
So what have your experiences with perception been?
Do you have any funny stories, too?
How do we work with this?
How do we stay curious about the things that we think are going on?
What if we're not in the McNay Museum?
**Participant:** The most amusing story I have about perception is swimming laps in a 50-meter pool.
And you swim, and you swim, you turn counterclockwise around, and so forth.
And so there's this man swimming clockwise.
So I ended up at the end with him at the same time.
He did, and he says, "What's wrong with everybody?
There's like ten people in the lane."
I don't know.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah, well, there's that self.
Yeah, that sort of self-concern.
Yeah, I must be right.
They must all be wrong.
**Participant:** Once I took an advanced first aid course, very involved.
It's like a hundred hours.
My mind, my life was very full of first aid.
So I started encountering immediately upon finishing this course and being credentialed and everything, I started immediately encountering first aid incidents.
You're getting involved in, you know.
This guy had an epileptic fit in the middle of a movie at the movie theater and stuff.
That was a great story.
This other time, and this all in rapid succession, I was walking through this kind of cul-de-sac-y neighborhood up there by Whatcom Falls Park.
And I saw these two guys, and it looked like there was a house being built, and maybe they were working on that.
And they were walking away from the house, they were walking down the street ahead of me.
And the one guy was rubbing the back of his head like this, and then at one point he got down on all fours, right in the gutter, and put his head down right near the curb.
And I was like, he's got a head concussion or something.
I took quite a few minutes thinking about whether I should say something.
So I did the thing where you go, "Hey, my name's Bob and I'm first aid.
Are you okay?"
He looks at me and goes, "Yeah, I'm fine.
What about you?"
And then I just realized that they were thinking about something, and he had been sighting along this curb.
He was trying to line something up in his eye, and I suddenly realized, oh, okay.
Yeah, you're trying to practice compassion.
Yeah, the perception was wrong.
Just looking for something that wasn't there.
I have one that probably has happened to almost everyone in this room.
Shortly after, well, I'd been practicing with the group for a while, and I went on my first weekend retreat up in Vancouver, and I was sitting pretty still and doing okay, I thought.
And toward the end of the weekend, I suddenly realized that I was doing great.
The periods just seemed like they whizzed by, and I said something to Kate McCandless, and she said, "Oh, we shortened those periods because of blah, blah, blah."
But I bet everyone here has experienced the period of zazen as being either a lot shorter or a lot longer than it actually is.
And one time, Kate fell asleep with a sandwich, and we had a 45-minute sit.
I kept looking at my watch.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah, time is interesting for a perception topic.
We all perceive time in different ways, very subjectively.
Anything you want to say about perception?
It doesn't have to be a charming story, but it's good thinking about how do we perceive.
**Participant:** I was going to follow up with a story about learning and not necessarily misapplying, but applying it to the exclusion of what was truly important in my environment.
I was planting trees up in northern British Columbia, one of the first all-female crews working with the all-male rangers, and at any rate, they took us into bear country.

And a lot of us girls were a little bit concerned about that, so we got lessons on this, that, and the other, and they point out, "Okay, here are bear scats, and there, seeing that hair on the branch there, that's where a bear was picking berries, and there, there's a pile of barf, whatever.
That's all bear stuff, and there's a print."
And so, anyway, to make a long story short, on the weekend, I went out with my then-boyfriend for a walk in the woods around [unclear: "Kinnemath"], and I was showing off, to put it quite bluntly.
You know, "See, here, there's bear scat, and there, there's bear hair, and there's a bear print, and there's this bear," and my nose was down.
And he tapped me on the shoulder, and he said, "And there's a bear."
What does the big, [unclear: "bear-knowledgeable, a-bearing"] say?
"Oh, oh, you've got a noise, and oh, God, I'd like to get out of here."
Can I have one more thing?

I've always wished, I have a special-needs son, Nathaniel is 23 now, but all through the time he's growing up, I have wished that I could perceive the world through his eyes, because he must see everything so differently.
He hears, but he can't talk.
He perseverates on things.

There can be a field filled with horses, and beautiful, you know, a mountain in the background, and Nathaniel notices a piece of trash that's beside the road. [unclear: "Who throw out a car?"] Bad, litter, well, we call them bug people, because we don't have a good site for littered bugs, so we call them bug people.
I just wish I could see the world through his eyes for 10 minutes.
Not a funny story, but definitely something about perception.
And compassion.

**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah, and of course, us neurotypical guys all just assume that everyone perceives things the same as us, so we all perceive things a little differently too, but yeah, all the more true, probably, for Nathaniel.
What's that world look like?
And how can we really meet somebody and help them and be with them if we don't know their world?
We can only do our best.
**Participant:** Well, I'll share something.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah, you can have the last word.
**Participant:** Okay, this is not a funny story either, but in February, I got my wallet stolen at the library.
I mean, not the library, but at the hospital, and everything was in that passport, as well as my debit and credit cards, and everything, the whole ball of bags.
Anyway, so it was a nightmare, and I'm still going through that.
And before that, I had no concern about stuff.
I didn't lock my door.
I get out of the car.
I never worried about it, and where I left my bag.
It was just like, I just trusted.
I had this sense of it, and my whole perception has changed now.
I lock my door the moment I leave, and I'm so maybe overly conscious now of having that.
So my perception of the world has changed in that sense.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** From that one [unclear: "revet"] change, yeah.
Yeah.

Yeah, it makes me think of one of my, we've been studying the precepts again, and one of my favorite things in there from Robert Aitken is the idea that the reason you lock your door, one reason to think about locking your doors is not to protect your stuff so much as you're protecting other people from making the mistake of stealing.
You're just taking care of people, for what it's worth.
So perception.
There's another perception thing.
How do we perceive and act?
What does it mean?
We give meanings to everything, too, which is sort of an act of perception.
Well, it's worth thinking about, so let's all think a little bit about, yeah, how are we making this world, from our senses and our ideas and our history, and what happens when it suddenly shifts.
